stem: The accounting rule 'anticipate no profit but provide for all possible losses' reflects the concept of:
explanation: Prudence or conservatism asks accountants to record expected losses but not expected gains, so that profits and assets are not overstated.

stem: A firm has total assets of ₹5,00,000 and outside liabilities of ₹1,80,000. According to the accounting equation, the owner's capital is:
explanation: Capital = Assets − Liabilities = ₹5,00,000 − ₹1,80,000 = ₹3,20,000. ₹6,80,000 wrongly adds the two figures.

stem: Assertion (A): Fixed assets are shown in the balance sheet at cost less depreciation rather than at their realisable value.
reason: Reason (R): The going concern assumption presumes that the business will continue to operate in the foreseeable future.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Both are true. Because the business is not expected to sell its fixed assets soon, their break-up (realisable) value does not matter, so going concern explains the cost-less-depreciation basis.

stem: Consider the following statements about accounting concepts:
items: Under the money measurement concept, only transactions that can be expressed in money are recorded.
The business entity concept treats the business as separate from its owner.
The matching concept requires expenses to be matched with the revenues of the same period.
Under the realisation concept, revenue is recognised only when cash is received.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1 to 3 are correct. Under the realisation concept revenue is recognised when it is earned, for example when goods are delivered, even if cash comes later.

stem: Match List I (accounting concept) with List II (example):
listII: Contingent liabilities shown in notes to accounts
Same depreciation method followed year after year
Wages due but unpaid recorded as an expense
A low-cost stapler written off as an expense when bought
explanation: Using the same method each year shows consistency; expensing a trivial item shows materiality; recording wages due shows accrual; showing contingent liabilities in notes shows full disclosure.

stem: Arrange the following steps of the accounting cycle in the correct order:
items: Preparing the trial balance
Recording in the journal
Preparing final accounts
Posting to the ledger
explanation: Transactions are first journalised, then posted to the ledger, then balanced into a trial balance, from which the final accounts are prepared.

stem: A and B share profits in the ratio 3:2. C is admitted and the new profit-sharing ratio of A, B and C is 5:3:2. The sacrificing ratio of A and B is:
explanation: Sacrifice = old share − new share. A: 3/5 − 5/10 = 6/10 − 5/10 = 1/10. B: 2/5 − 3/10 = 4/10 − 3/10 = 1/10. So the sacrificing ratio is 1:1.

stem: Under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, when the partnership deed says nothing on the matter, interest on partners' capital is:
options: Allowed at 6 per cent per annum
Allowed at 5 per cent per annum
explanation: Without an agreement, partners are not entitled to interest on capital. The 6 per cent rate applies to loans and advances a partner makes to the firm, not to capital.

stem: Assertion (A): On the admission of a new partner, accumulated reserves are shared among the old partners in their old profit-sharing ratio.
reason: Reason (R): Such reserves were built up out of profits earned when only the old partners shared profits in the old ratio.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Both are true. The reserves belong to the old partners because they come from past profits those partners shared in the old ratio, so R explains A.

stem: Consider the following statements about the rule in Garner v. Murray:
items: Solvent partners bear the capital deficiency of an insolvent partner in the ratio of their capitals.
The rule applies only when there is no agreement to the contrary among the partners.
Solvent partners must bring in cash equal to their share of the loss on realisation.
Under the rule, the insolvent partner's deficiency is shared in the profit-sharing ratio.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1 to 3 are correct. Garner v. Murray shares the deficiency in the ratio of capitals, not in the profit-sharing ratio, so statement 4 is wrong.

stem: Match List I (item in partnership accounts) with List II (description):
listII: Old share minus new share of existing partners
Insurance on the lives of all partners, payable on the death of any one
Opened to close the books of the firm on dissolution
New share minus old share of continuing partners
explanation: The gaining ratio (new minus old share) applies to continuing partners; the sacrificing ratio (old minus new share) applies on admission; the realisation account is used on dissolution; a joint life policy pays out on the death of any partner.

stem: Under Section 48 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, arrange the order in which the firm's assets are applied on dissolution:
items: Paying each partner what is due on account of capital
Distributing any residue among partners in their profit-sharing ratio
Paying debts of the firm to third parties
Paying each partner's loans and advances to the firm
explanation: Section 48 requires third-party debts to be paid first, then partners' loans and advances, then partners' capital, and finally any surplus in the profit-sharing ratio.

stem: When forfeited shares are reissued, the balance left in the share forfeiture account on those shares is transferred to:
explanation: The profit on reissue of forfeited shares is a capital profit, so it is transferred to capital reserve.

stem: H Ltd acquired 80 per cent of the equity shares of S Ltd for ₹5,20,000. On the date of acquisition, S Ltd had share capital of ₹5,00,000 and reserves of ₹1,00,000. Goodwill or capital reserve on consolidation is:
explanation: H's share of net assets = 80% × (5,00,000 + 1,00,000) = ₹4,80,000. Cost ₹5,20,000 − ₹4,80,000 = ₹40,000 paid in excess, which is goodwill. ₹1,20,000 is the non-controlling interest, not goodwill.

stem: Assertion (A): Under AS 14, an amalgamation in the nature of purchase is accounted for using the purchase method.
reason: Reason (R): Under the pooling of interests method, assets and liabilities of the transferor company are recorded at their existing carrying amounts.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Both are true. R describes the pooling of interests method, which is used for amalgamations in the nature of merger, so it does not explain why the purchase method is used for purchase-type amalgamations.

stem: Consider the following statements under the Companies Act, 2013:
items: Securities premium can be used to issue fully paid bonus shares.
Securities premium can be distributed to shareholders as dividend.
Calls in arrears are deducted from called-up capital in the balance sheet.
Redeemable preference shares can be redeemed only out of distributable profits or the proceeds of a fresh issue of shares.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct. Securities premium is a capital receipt and can be used only for the purposes allowed by Section 52; paying dividends is not one of them.

stem: Consider the following statements about internal reconstruction:
items: It usually involves a reduction of share capital.
The capital reduction account is used to write off accumulated losses and fictitious assets.
The existing company is wound up and a new company is formed to take over its business.
Any balance left in the capital reduction account is transferred to capital reserve.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Winding up the old company and forming a new one is external reconstruction; in internal reconstruction the same company carries on.

stem: Match List I (term) with List II (context in corporate accounting):
listII: Internal reconstruction
Consolidated financial statements
Amalgamation
Winding up of a company
explanation: Purchase consideration arises in amalgamation, the liquidator's final statement in winding up, non-controlling interest in consolidation, and the capital reduction account in internal reconstruction.

stem: Fixed costs are ₹1,20,000, the selling price is ₹50 per unit and the variable cost is ₹30 per unit. The break-even point in units is:
explanation: Contribution per unit = 50 − 30 = ₹20. BEP = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit = 1,20,000 ÷ 20 = 6,000 units, or sales of ₹3,00,000. 2,400 units wrongly divides by the selling price.

stem: Sales are ₹5,00,000, the P/V ratio is 40 per cent and fixed costs are ₹1,20,000. The margin of safety is:
Assertion (A): Under marginal costing, closing stock is valued at variable cost only.
reason: Reason (R): Under marginal costing, fixed manufacturing overheads are treated as period costs and charged in full to the period in which they arise.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Both are true. Because fixed overheads are written off as period costs, none of them is carried forward in inventory, which is why stock is valued at variable cost. R explains A.

stem: Consider the following statements about variance analysis in standard costing:
items: Material cost variance equals material price variance plus material usage variance.
Labour efficiency variance equals standard rate × (standard hours for actual output − actual hours worked).
Labour idle time variance can be favourable.
Material price variance equals standard price × (standard quantity − actual quantity).
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Idle time means paying for hours with no output, so it is always adverse. The formula in statement 4 is the material usage variance; the price variance is actual quantity × (standard price − actual price).

stem: Consider the following statements about process costing:
items: The cost of normal loss is absorbed by the good units produced.
Abnormal loss is valued like good units and transferred to the costing profit and loss account.
Equivalent production expresses partly finished units as an equal number of fully completed units.
Abnormal gain raises the cost per unit of good output.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1 to 3 are correct. Abnormal gain is valued at the normal cost per unit and credited to costing profit and loss, so it does not raise the cost per unit of good output.

stem: Arrange the following steps in preparing a process account with work-in-progress in the correct order:
items: Computing cost per equivalent unit
Valuing completed units and closing work-in-progress
Preparing the statement of physical flow of units
Preparing the statement of equivalent production
explanation: Physical units are first reconciled, then converted into equivalent units, cost per equivalent unit is worked out, and finally completed output and closing WIP are valued.

stem: Zero-base budgeting was developed and popularised by:
explanation: Peter Pyhrr developed zero-base budgeting at Texas Instruments around 1970. Kaplan is linked with ABC and the balanced scorecard, Ohno with the Toyota Production System, and Imai with kaizen.

stem: Assertion (A): Target costing is mainly a cost-control technique applied after production of a product has started.
reason: Reason (R): Target cost is found by deducting the desired profit margin from the competitive market price.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is false: target costing is applied at the product planning and design stage, where most costs are locked in. R correctly states how target cost is calculated.

stem: Assertion (A): Kaizen costing aims at continuous, small cost reductions during the manufacturing stage of a product.
reason: Reason (R): Kaizen costing is applied mainly at the product design stage before production begins.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is true. R is false: the design stage is where target costing applies, while kaizen costing works on continuous improvement during production.

stem: Consider the following statements about budgets:
items: A flexible budget stays the same whatever the level of activity.
A cash budget is a functional budget.
The master budget is a summary of all functional budgets.
A fixed budget is most suitable where activity levels fluctuate widely.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. A flexible budget is adjusted to different activity levels, and a fixed budget suits stable activity, so statements 1 and 4 are wrong.

stem: Match List I (technique) with List II (main feature):
listII: Every activity is justified afresh at each budget
Overheads assigned through multiple cost drivers
Costs tracked from design to final disposal of the product
Continuous improvement during the production stage
explanation: ABC uses cost drivers, life-cycle costing covers a product's whole life, kaizen costing seeks continuous improvement in production, and ZBB justifies every activity from zero.

stem: Arrange the following steps of budgetary control in the correct order:
items: Preparing budgets
Taking corrective action
Comparing actual performance with the budget
Setting organisational objectives
explanation: Objectives are set first, budgets are prepared to meet them, actual results are compared with the budget, and corrective action is taken on the variances.

stem: A firm's current ratio is 2.5 and its working capital is ₹60,000. Its current assets are:
explanation: Let current liabilities = x, so current assets = 2.5x. Working capital = 2.5x − x = 1.5x = 60,000, so x = ₹40,000 and current assets = 2.5 × 40,000 = ₹1,00,000.

stem: Assertion (A): In the indirect method, depreciation is added back to net profit to find cash flow from operating activities.
reason: Reason (R): Depreciation is itself a source of cash for the business.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is true because depreciation is a non-cash expense that reduced net profit. R is false: depreciation does not bring in any cash; it is only added back because no cash went out.

stem: Assertion (A): The quick ratio is a stricter test of liquidity than the current ratio.
reason: Reason (R): A current ratio of 2:1 is conventionally regarded as satisfactory.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Both are true, but the 2:1 norm does not explain A. The quick ratio is stricter because it leaves out inventory and prepaid expenses, which are harder to turn into cash.

stem: Under AS 3 / Ind AS 7, consider the following classifications in the cash flow statement of a non-financial company:
items: Purchase of machinery is an investing activity.
Payment to suppliers of goods is a financing activity.
Issue of debentures is a financing activity.
Buy-back of equity shares is a financing activity.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct. Payments to suppliers relate to the main revenue-producing activity, so they are operating cash flows.

stem: Match List I (ratio) with List II (formula):
listII: EBIT ÷ Interest
EBIT ÷ Capital employed
Cost of goods sold ÷ Average inventory
Long-term debt ÷ Shareholders' funds
explanation: Inventory turnover is COGS over average inventory, debt-equity is long-term debt over shareholders' funds, interest coverage is EBIT over interest, and ROCE is EBIT over capital employed.

stem: A firm has sales of ₹10,00,000, gross profit of ₹2,50,000 and operating expenses of ₹1,50,000 (no other income or expenses). Arrange the following ratios in ascending order of value:
items: Operating ratio
Net profit ratio
Gross profit ratio
Operating expense ratio

stem: The Lev and Schwartz model of human resource accounting values employees on the basis of:
options: Present value of their future earnings
Historical cost of recruitment and training
explanation: Lev and Schwartz value human capital as the present value of employees' future earnings until retirement. Competitive bidding (opportunity cost) is the Hekimian and Jones approach.

stem: Under the Current Purchasing Power (CPP) method of inflation accounting, historical figures are restated using:
options: Specific price indices of individual assets
explanation: CPP converts historical amounts into units of current purchasing power using a general price index such as the consumer price index. Specific indices and replacement cost are used in current cost accounting.

stem: Assertion (A): Under CPP accounting, holding monetary liabilities during a period of inflation results in a loss of purchasing power.
reason: Reason (R): Monetary items are fixed in money terms regardless of changes in the price level.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is false: a firm that owes a fixed money amount repays it in money of lower purchasing power, so it gains. R is true, and it is the reason monetary liabilities produce a gain.

stem: Consider the following statements:
items: Environmental accounting identifies and reports the environmental costs and benefits of a firm's activities.
Human resource accounting treats employees as assets of the organisation.
Disclosure of human resource accounts is mandatory for all companies under the Companies Act, 2013.
Flamholtz proposed a stochastic rewards valuation model for human resources.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. HRA disclosure is voluntary in India; firms such as BHEL and Infosys have reported it on their own.

stem: Match List I (human resource valuation approach) with List II (proponent):
listII: Jaggi and Lau
Eric Flamholtz
Hekimian and Jones
Lev and Schwartz
explanation: Lev and Schwartz proposed the present value model, Hekimian and Jones the opportunity cost model, Flamholtz the stochastic rewards model, and Jaggi and Lau the group valuation model.

stem: Under CPP accounting, the general price index is 200 at year end. Arrange the following in ascending order of their CPP-restated year-end values:
items: Land bought for ₹50,000 when the index was 100
Machinery bought for ₹90,000 when the index was 150
Furniture bought for ₹70,000 when the index was 175
Cash balance of ₹1,10,000 at year end

stem: Ind AS 115 deals with:
explanation: Ind AS 115 covers revenue from contracts with customers. Leases fall under Ind AS 116, financial instruments under Ind AS 109, and PPE under Ind AS 16.

stem: International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) are issued by the:
explanation: The IASB, under the IFRS Foundation, issues IFRS. The FASB sets US GAAP, and IFAC issues auditing and ethics standards through its boards.

stem: Assertion (A): Ind AS are word-for-word identical to IFRS, with no carve-outs.
reason: Reason (R): Ind AS are standards converged with IFRS.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is false: Ind AS are converged with IFRS but include some carve-outs and carve-ins to suit Indian conditions. R is true.

stem: Consider the following statements about Indian Accounting Standards:
items: Ind AS 116 requires a lessee to recognise a right-of-use asset for most leases.
Ind AS 2 allows the LIFO method for valuing inventories.
Ind AS 16 allows the revaluation model for property, plant and equipment.
Ind AS 36 deals with impairment of assets.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct. Ind AS 2, like IAS 2, does not allow LIFO; FIFO or weighted average cost must be used.

stem: Match List I (Ind AS) with List II (subject):
listII: Income taxes
Statement of cash flows
Consolidated financial statements
Intangible assets
explanation: Ind AS 7 covers cash flows, Ind AS 12 income taxes, Ind AS 38 intangible assets, and Ind AS 110 consolidated financial statements.

stem: Arrange the following steps of the revenue recognition model under Ind AS 115 in the correct order:
items: Identify the performance obligations
Allocate the transaction price to the performance obligations
Identify the contract with the customer
Determine the transaction price
explanation: The five-step model is: identify the contract, identify the performance obligations, determine the transaction price, allocate it, and recognise revenue as each obligation is satisfied.

stem: Vouching in auditing means:
options: Examining documentary evidence that supports recorded transactions
Physically verifying the existence of assets
Checking the valuation of assets at the balance sheet date
Checking the arithmetic accuracy of totals
explanation: Vouching tests the authenticity of entries by checking them against vouchers such as invoices and receipts. Checking existence and valuation of assets is verification and valuation.

stem: Under SA 705, an auditor issues an adverse opinion when misstatements in the financial statements are:
options: Possibly material and pervasive but sufficient evidence cannot be obtained
Not material, individually or in total
explanation: Material and pervasive misstatement leads to an adverse opinion. Material but not pervasive leads to a qualified opinion, and inability to get sufficient evidence with possibly pervasive effects leads to a disclaimer.

stem: Assertion (A): Verification involves confirming the existence, ownership and valuation of assets.
reason: Reason (R): Verification is concerned only with checking the arithmetic accuracy of the books of account.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is true. R is false: verification is about the existence, title and value of assets and liabilities, not about arithmetic accuracy.

stem: Consider the following statements under the Companies Act, 2013:
items: The statutory auditor of a non-government company is appointed by the shareholders at the annual general meeting.
The auditor of a government company is appointed by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India.
The internal auditor of a company may also be appointed as its statutory auditor.
SA 700 deals with forming an opinion and reporting on financial statements.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. An employee of the company is disqualified under Section 141, and Section 144 bars the statutory auditor from providing internal audit services, so the two roles cannot be combined.

stem: Match List I (Standard on Auditing) with List II (subject):
listII: Audit evidence
Forming an opinion and reporting on financial statements
Audit documentation
Overall objectives of the independent auditor
explanation: SA 200 sets the overall objectives of the independent auditor, SA 230 covers audit documentation, SA 500 audit evidence, and SA 700 forming an opinion and reporting.

stem: Arrange the following stages of an audit in the correct order:
items: Issuing the audit report
Planning the audit
Agreeing the terms of engagement
Collecting audit evidence
explanation: The auditor first agrees the terms of engagement, then plans the audit, then gathers evidence, and finally issues the report.

stem: Under Section 148 of the Companies Act, 2013, the cost audit of a company must be conducted by a:
explanation: Section 148(3) requires the cost audit to be done by a cost accountant in practice, and the company's statutory auditor cannot be appointed as its cost auditor.

stem: The main purpose of a forensic audit is to:
options: Give an opinion on whether the financial statements are true and fair
Assess how efficiently the cost of production is controlled
Check that the company has complied with tax laws
Detect fraud and gather evidence that can be used in legal proceedings
explanation: A forensic audit investigates suspected fraud or misconduct and gathers evidence for courts. A true and fair opinion is the goal of a statutory audit.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Companies Act, 2013, the Central Government may order a cost audit for specified classes of companies.
reason: Reason (R): A person appointed as the statutory auditor of a company under Section 139 cannot be appointed as its cost auditor.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Both are true under Section 148. But the bar on the statutory auditor being the cost auditor does not explain why the government orders cost audits for certain companies.

stem: Consider the following statements about recent trends in auditing:
items: Continuous auditing uses technology to give assurance close to real time.
Computer-assisted audit techniques (CAATs) help auditors analyse large volumes of data.
Blockchain can make audit trails harder to alter.
Environmental audit is mandatory for all companies under the Companies Act, 2013.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1 to 3 are correct. The Companies Act, 2013 does not require an environmental audit for all companies.

stem: Match List I (type of audit) with List II (focus):
listII: Whether expenditure is justified and in the public interest
Contribution of the firm to social objectives
Best use of resources to achieve results
Appraisal of the performance of management
explanation: An efficiency audit checks whether resources are used well, a propriety audit checks whether spending is justified, a management audit appraises management performance, and a social audit reviews social contribution.

stem: Arrange the following steps of a statutory cost audit under the Companies Act, 2013 in the correct order:
items: Cost auditor submits the cost audit report to the Board
Company files the cost audit report with the Central Government
Board appoints the cost auditor on the recommendation of the audit committee
Cost auditor audits the cost records
explanation: The Board first appoints the cost auditor, the auditor audits the cost records and sends the report to the Board, and the company then files the report with the Central Government.

stem: Goods taken by the proprietor from the business for his personal use are recorded by debiting:
explanation: Withdrawal of goods for personal use is a drawing; the drawings account is debited and the purchases (or stock) account is credited.

stem: Expenses incurred on repairing a second-hand machine just after purchase, to make it fit for use, are treated as:
explanation: Costs needed to bring an asset into working condition are part of its cost, hence capital expenditure.

stem: A machine costing ₹2,00,000 is depreciated at 10 per cent per annum on the written down value method. Depreciation for the second year is:

Item X has cost ₹50,000 and net realisable value ₹45,000; item Y has cost ₹30,000 and net realisable value ₹36,000. Applying the 'lower of cost and net realisable value' rule item by item, closing stock is valued at:
A debt written off as bad in an earlier year is recovered in the current year. The amount recovered is treated as:
options: A reduction in the current year's bad debts provision only
A capital receipt credited to capital account
A fresh credit sale to the debtor
Income of the current year credited to bad debts recovered account
explanation: Recovery of a debt already written off is an item of gain; it is credited to bad debts recovered account and appears as income of the year of recovery.

stem: Under the IASB's Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting, the fundamental qualitative characteristics of useful financial information are:
explanation: Relevance and faithful representation are the fundamental characteristics; comparability, verifiability, timeliness and understandability are enhancing characteristics.

stem: The cash book shows a favourable balance of ₹50,000. Cheques of ₹8,000 issued to suppliers have not yet been presented, and cheques of ₹5,000 deposited have not yet been collected by the bank. The balance as per pass book is:
explanation: Start from cash book: add back cheques issued but not presented (+8,000) and deduct cheques deposited but not yet credited (−5,000). 50,000 + 8,000 − 5,000 = ₹53,000.

stem: The fundamental accounting assumptions recognised in AS 1 (Disclosure of Accounting Policies) are:
options: Consistency, prudence and substance over form
explanation: AS 1 treats going concern, consistency and accrual as fundamental assumptions; prudence, substance over form and materiality guide the selection of policies.

stem: The principle that every transaction has two equal and opposite aspects, which forms the basis of the double-entry system, is called the:
explanation: Dual aspect means each transaction affects two accounts, with an equal debit and credit, which is why double entry works.

stem: A sale of ₹4,000 to Mohan was correctly entered in the sales book but posted to Mohan's account as ₹400. To make the trial balance agree, the suspense account will initially be:
explanation: Debit side shows 400 instead of 4,000, so debits are short by ₹3,600; suspense account is debited with ₹3,600 and later cleared by debiting Mohan's account.

stem: Assertion (A): Outstanding rent for the last month of the year is recorded as an expense and a liability in that year's accounts.
reason: Reason (R): Under the accrual basis, expenses are recognised when incurred, irrespective of when cash is paid.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Accrual accounting records an expense when it is incurred, so unpaid rent of the year is an expense and a liability of that year; R is the reason.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the cost concept, fixed assets are revalued every year to show their current market value.
reason: Reason (R): The cost concept records an asset at the price paid at the time of its acquisition.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is false because the cost concept keeps assets at acquisition cost (less depreciation), not at market value. R is a correct statement of the concept.

stem: Assertion (A): Expenditure on a one-year advertising campaign is treated as revenue expenditure.
reason: Reason (R): Capital expenditure is charged wholly to the profit and loss account of the year in which it is incurred.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is true as the benefit is consumed within the year. R is false: capital expenditure is capitalised and spread over the asset's life through depreciation.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the accrual basis, a credit sale is recognised as revenue in the period in which the sale is made.
reason: Reason (R): Under the money measurement concept, only transactions that can be expressed in money are recorded.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Both statements are true, but money measurement concerns what is recorded, not when revenue is recognised, so R does not explain A.

stem: Assertion (A): The consistency concept prohibits any change in accounting policy under all circumstances.
reason: Reason (R): AS 1 permits a change in an accounting policy if required by a statute or an accounting standard, or if it gives a more appropriate presentation.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is false: consistency means policies are not changed arbitrarily, but changes are allowed in the situations stated in R, which is true.

stem: Assertion (A): Depreciation is charged even on an asset whose market value is rising.
reason: Reason (R): Depreciation is an allocation of an asset's cost over its useful life and is not a process of valuation.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Because depreciation allocates cost rather than tracking market value, it continues even if market value rises. R explains A.

stem: Consider the following statements about the rules of debit and credit:
items: For a real account, debit what comes in and credit what goes out.
For a nominal account, debit expenses and losses and credit incomes and gains.
For a personal account, credit the receiver and debit the giver.
The capital account of a proprietor is a nominal account.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1 and 2 are the standard rules. Under the personal account rule the receiver is debited and the giver credited; capital is a personal account, not nominal.

stem: Consider the following statements about capital and revenue expenditure:
items: Legal fees paid to acquire land are capital expenditure.
Wages paid for installing a new machine are capital expenditure.
Repairs to keep existing machinery in working order are capital expenditure.
Heavy advertising whose benefit extends over several years is deferred revenue expenditure.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Costs to acquire or install an asset are capital; routine repairs are revenue; benefits spread over several years make advertising deferred revenue expenditure.

stem: Consider the following statements about errors in accounting:
items: Compensating errors do not disturb the agreement of the trial balance.
An error of principle does not disturb the agreement of the trial balance.
An error of commission always disturbs the agreement of the trial balance.
A balance in the suspense account shows that some errors are yet to be located.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Posting to a wrong account (commission) may leave the trial balance in agreement; statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct.

stem: Consider the following statements based on the accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Capital):
items: Drawings by the proprietor reduce capital.
Purchase of goods on credit increases both assets and liabilities.
Payment to a creditor in cash reduces both assets and liabilities.
Payment of salary in cash reduces assets and increases liabilities.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Salary paid in cash reduces assets and reduces capital (through an expense); liabilities do not rise.

stem: Consider the following statements about bases of accounting:
items: Under the cash basis, income is recorded when cash is received.
Under the accrual basis, outstanding expenses are ignored until they are paid.
Under the accrual basis, income earned but not yet received is recorded.
Under the Companies Act, 2013, a company must keep its books on the accrual basis and the double-entry system.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Accrual accounting records outstanding expenses; statement 2 is false. The other three are correct.

stem: Consider the following statements about substance over form and materiality:
items: Substance over form means transactions are recorded strictly according to their legal form.
Under AS 19, a lessee records an asset acquired on finance lease even though legal title stays with the lessor.
An item is material if its omission or misstatement could influence the economic decisions of users.
Materiality is an absolute amount fixed by law for all businesses.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Substance over form gives priority to economic reality; the finance lease is an example. Materiality depends on the item's nature and size, not a statutory fixed sum.

stem: Match List I (rule or principle) with List II (statement):
listII: Debit the receiver, credit the giver
Debit what comes in, credit what goes out
Debit expenses and losses, credit incomes and gains
Every transaction has an equal debit and credit effect
explanation: Each rule is matched to its standard statement.

stem: Match List I (accounting concept) with List II (illustration):
listII: Financial statements are prepared at regular intervals
Owner's capital is shown as a claim of the owner on the business
Machine recorded at the price actually paid, not its market value
Skill of the workforce is not recorded in the books
explanation: Entity concept separates the owner from the business; money measurement excludes non-monetary facts; cost concept uses acquisition price; periodicity gives yearly reporting.

stem: Match List I (depreciation method) with List II (feature):
listII: Annual amounts are invested outside to replace the asset
Equal amount charged every year
Fixed percentage applied on the opening book value
Interest on the money invested in the asset is also taken into account
explanation: These are the standard distinguishing features of each depreciation method.

stem: Match List I (type of error) with List II (illustration):
listII: Sale to Ram posted to Rahim's account
A credit sale never entered in any book
Excess debit in one account offset by an equal excess credit in another
Purchase of furniture debited to purchases account
explanation: Each illustration is the textbook example of the stated error type.

stem: Arrange the following in the order in which they are prepared for a manufacturing concern:
items: Balance sheet
Manufacturing account
Profit and loss account
Trading account
explanation: Cost of production is found first, then gross profit, then net profit, and finally the balance sheet.

stem: Arrange the following year-end steps of a sole proprietor in the correct order:
items: Transfer sales and purchases balances to the trading account to find gross profit
Show the closing capital in the balance sheet
Transfer gross profit to the profit and loss account
Transfer net profit to the capital account
explanation: Gross profit is found first, then net profit, then capital is adjusted and shown in the balance sheet.

stem: Arrange the following events in the accounting life of a machine in the correct order:
items: Charging depreciation every year
Recording the machine at cost
Recognising the profit or loss on disposal
Transferring the book value to the asset disposal account on sale
explanation: The asset is capitalised, depreciated over use, then transferred on sale, and the disposal result is finally recognised.

stem: A firm's profits for the last three years were ₹60,000, ₹70,000 and ₹80,000. Goodwill valued at two years' purchase of the average profit is:
Capital employed in a firm is ₹5,00,000, the normal rate of return is 10 per cent and the average profit is ₹80,000. Goodwill at three years' purchase of super profit is:

A and B have total capital and reserves of ₹5,00,000 and the net assets of the firm are ₹5,00,000. C is admitted for a one-fourth share and brings ₹2,00,000 as capital. The goodwill of the firm implied by C's contribution is:
explanation: C's 1/4 share is worth 2,00,000, so total firm capital = 8,00,000. Net assets after admission = 5,00,000 + 2,00,000 = 7,00,000. Goodwill = 8,00,000 − 7,00,000 = ₹1,00,000.

stem: A, B and C share profits in the ratio 4:3:2. C retires and A and B decide to share future profits equally. The gaining ratio of A and B is:
explanation: A's old share 4/9, new 1/2: gain = 1/2 − 4/9 = 1/18. B's old 3/9 = 1/3, new 1/2: gain = 1/6 = 3/18. Gaining ratio = 1:3 (total 4/18 = C's 2/9).

stem: Under Section 37 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, if the business is continued without settling the account of a deceased partner, his legal representatives are entitled, at their option, to share of profits attributable to the use of his share of property or to interest at:
options: 5 per cent per annum on the amount due
6 per cent per annum on the amount due
The bank rate on the amount due
9 per cent per annum on the amount due
explanation: Section 37 gives the outgoing partner or his estate the option of attributable profits or interest at 6 per cent per annum on his share in the firm's property.

stem: On dissolution, the book value of non-cash assets is ₹3,00,000 and they realise ₹2,60,000; outside creditors of ₹80,000 are settled for ₹78,000, and realisation expenses of ₹4,000 are paid. The loss on realisation is:
explanation: Debit side: assets 3,00,000 + creditors paid 78,000 + expenses 4,000 = 3,82,000. Credit side: creditors 80,000 + cash from assets 2,60,000 = 3,40,000. Loss = ₹42,000.

stem: Under the fixed capital method, a partner's share of profit, interest on capital and salary are recorded in his:
explanation: With fixed capital, the capital account stays unchanged and all such adjustments pass through the partner's current account.

stem: A and B share profits 3:2. On the admission of C, stock is appreciated by ₹12,000, building is depreciated by ₹4,000 and a provision for doubtful debts of ₹2,000 is created. A's share of the profit on revaluation is:
explanation: Net revaluation profit = 12,000 − 4,000 − 2,000 = 6,000. It is shared in the old ratio 3:2, so A gets 6,000 × 3/5 = ₹3,600.

stem: Under Section 30 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, a minor admitted to the benefits of a partnership is:
options: Personally liable for all debts like other partners
Liable only for debts arising after he attains majority
Entitled to bind the firm by his acts
Not personally liable for the firm's debts beyond his share in the firm's property and profits
explanation: A minor is not personally liable; his liability is limited to his share in the profits and property of the firm.

stem: Assertion (A): When a new partner pays a premium for goodwill, it is credited to the old partners in their sacrificing ratio.
reason: Reason (R): The old partners who sacrifice part of their share of future profits in favour of the new partner are entitled to compensation.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Goodwill premium compensates the partners who give up profit share, so it goes to them in the sacrificing ratio; R explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): In the absence of any agreement, partners share profits in the ratio of their capital contributions.
reason: Reason (R): Under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, partners share profits equally when the deed is silent.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is false: the Act provides equal sharing irrespective of capital. R is a correct statement of the default rule.

stem: Assertion (A): A retiring partner continues to be liable for the firm's debts incurred before his retirement, unless the creditors agree to discharge him.
reason: Reason (R): A retiring partner remains liable for acts done after retirement until public notice of retirement is given.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Both statements reflect Section 32, but R deals with post-retirement acts and does not explain A.

stem: Assertion (A): A revaluation account is prepared on the retirement of a partner.
reason: Reason (R): The balance of the revaluation account is transferred to the capital accounts of the partners in the new profit-sharing ratio.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is true as assets and liabilities are revalued. R is false: the revaluation profit or loss belongs to the old partners and is shared in the old ratio.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the fluctuating capital method, a partner's capital account balance changes from year to year.
reason: Reason (R): Under this method, profits, interest, salary and drawings are all adjusted through the capital account.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: All adjustments pass through the capital account, which therefore fluctuates; R explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): A partner's liability for the debts of the firm is joint and several and unlimited.
reason: Reason (R): Under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, a partner's liability is limited to the capital contributed by him.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is true under Section 25. R is false: liability extends to the partner's private property, not only his capital.

stem: Consider the following statements about the Indian Partnership Act, 1932:
items: Compulsory dissolution takes place when all the partners, or all but one, are adjudged insolvent.
Compulsory dissolution takes place when the business becomes unlawful.
The death of a partner always dissolves the firm, even if the deed says otherwise.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Section 41 covers insolvency and illegality. Death of a partner dissolves the firm only subject to a contrary agreement.

stem: Consider the following statements about the valuation of goodwill:
items: In the average profit method, goodwill is average profit multiplied by the agreed number of years' purchase.
Super profit is the excess of actual average profit over normal profit.
Under the capitalisation method, goodwill is the capitalised value of average profit less the actual capital employed.
Goodwill need not be valued when a partner retires.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: The first three describe standard methods; goodwill must be valued on retirement to compensate the retiring partner.

stem: Consider the following statements regarding partners' rights when the deed is silent:
items: Partners share profits and losses equally.
A partner is entitled to a salary for taking part in the business.
A partner is entitled to interest at 6 per cent per annum on capital contributed.
A partner who lends money to the firm beyond his capital is entitled to interest at 6 per cent per annum.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Without agreement, no salary and no interest on capital are allowed; interest at 6 per cent is allowed only on advances beyond capital.

stem: Consider the following statements about the retirement of a partner:
items: The retiring partner's share of goodwill is debited to the gaining partners' capital accounts in the gaining ratio.
Profit or loss on revaluation is shared in the old profit-sharing ratio.
The amount due may be transferred to a loan account if not paid immediately.
The amount due to a retiring partner must always be paid at once in cash.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Payment may be deferred through a loan account, so statement 4 is wrong; statements 1 to 3 are standard treatment.

stem: Consider the following statements about the realisation account on dissolution:
items: Assets are transferred to it at their realisable values.
Cash realised from the sale of assets is credited to it.
Expenses of dissolution paid by the firm are debited to it.
Loss on realisation is shared by the partners in the ratio of their capitals.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Assets go to the realisation account at book values, and loss is shared in the profit-sharing ratio; statements 2 and 3 are correct.

stem: Consider the following statements about partnership:
items: Mutual agency is an essential feature of partnership.
A partnership firm has a legal personality separate from its partners.
A partnership can be created by an oral agreement.
Partnership arises from contract and not from status.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Under the Act a firm is not a legal entity distinct from its partners; the other statements are correct.

stem: Match List I (method) with List II (formula):
listII: Average profit × number of years' purchase
(Average profit − normal profit) × years' purchase
Value of the firm implied by the new partner's share, less net assets
Average profit × 100 / normal rate, less capital employed
explanation: Each valuation approach is matched with its characteristic formula.

stem: Match List I (provision of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932) with List II (subject):
listII: Right of outgoing partner to share in subsequent profits
Definition of partnership
Effect of non-registration of a firm
Joint and several liability of partners
explanation: These are the sections dealing with the stated subjects.

stem: Match List I (account) with List II (purpose):
listII: Records the disposal of assets and settlement of liabilities on dissolution
Records profit share, interest and drawings under the fixed capital method
Records changes in values of assets and liabilities on a change in the firm's constitution
Shows distribution of net profit among partners
explanation: Each account serves the stated purpose in partnership accounting.

stem: Match List I (term) with List II (meaning):
listII: Change in the relationship of partners while the business may continue
Arises on insolvency of all partners or illegality of the business
Partnership with no fixed duration or particular undertaking
Business closes, assets are realised and liabilities paid
explanation: These are the standard meanings of the terms.

stem: Arrange the following steps on dissolution of a firm in the correct order:
items: Transferring non-cash assets and outside liabilities to the realisation account
Closing partners' capital accounts by final payment
Recording the sale of assets
Paying outside liabilities and realisation expenses
explanation: Assets and liabilities are first transferred, assets are sold, liabilities settled, and partners are finally paid.

stem: Arrange the following steps in dealing with goodwill on admission of a partner in the correct order:
items: Fix the new profit-sharing ratio
Distribute the goodwill premium among the sacrificing partners
Ascertain the old profit-sharing ratio
Compute the sacrificing ratio
explanation: The sacrificing ratio needs the old and new ratios, and the premium is shared in that ratio.

stem: Arrange the following steps in computing goodwill by the super profit method:
items: Find the average profit
Multiply super profit by the number of years' purchase
Find the normal profit on capital employed
Find the super profit
explanation: Super profit = average profit − normal profit, and goodwill = super profit × years' purchase.

stem: Arrange the following steps in finding the profit of a deceased partner up to the date of his death (time basis):
items: Take the profit of the previous year
Apportion it for the period from the last balance sheet date to the date of death
Credit the result to the deceased partner's account
Multiply by the deceased partner's profit share
explanation: Profit of the previous year is time-apportioned, then multiplied by the share and credited.

stem: A company offered 80,000 shares and received applications for 1,20,000 shares, which were allotted pro rata. An applicant who applied for 6,000 shares will be allotted:
explanation: Pro rata ratio = 80,000 : 1,20,000 = 2 : 3. Allotment = 6,000 × 2/3 = 4,000 shares; the remaining application money is adjusted or refunded.

stem: 100 shares of ₹10 each issued at par, on which ₹8 has been called and ₹5 per share received, are forfeited. The amount credited to the share forfeiture account is:
explanation: The share forfeiture account is credited with the amount actually received: 100 × ₹5 = ₹500. Share capital is debited with the called-up ₹800 and calls in arrears is credited with ₹300.

stem: Under Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013, the buy-back of shares in a financial year cannot exceed what proportion of the aggregate of paid-up capital and free reserves?
explanation: Section 68 caps a buy-back at 25 per cent of the aggregate of the company's paid-up capital and free reserves.

stem: Redeemable preference shares of ₹5,00,000 are redeemed at a 10 per cent premium. A fresh issue of equity shares of ₹3,00,000 at par is made for the purpose, and the rest is paid out of profits. The amount to be transferred to capital redemption reserve is:
explanation: CRR = nominal value redeemed (5,00,000) less proceeds of fresh issue (3,00,000) = ₹2,00,000. The premium is not part of the CRR computation.

stem: H Ltd holds 75 per cent of S Ltd. S Ltd has share capital of ₹10,00,000 and reserves of ₹2,00,000. The minority interest in S Ltd's net worth is:
In the winding up of a company limited by shares, the liability of a member is limited to:
options: The nominal value of the company's total capital
His share of the company's total debts
The market value of his shares
The amount unpaid on the shares held by him
explanation: A shareholder of a company limited by shares is a contributory only for the unpaid amount on his shares.

stem: A company issues 40,000 equity shares of face value ₹10 at ₹12 each and pays ₹1,00,000 in cash to the vendor company. The purchase consideration (payment method) is:
explanation: Consideration = shares at their issue value (40,000 × 12 = 4,80,000) + cash 1,00,000 = ₹5,80,000.

stem: Under Section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013, a reduction of share capital becomes effective only after confirmation by the:
options: Securities and Exchange Board of India
Institute of Chartered Accountants of India
explanation: Reduction of share capital needs a special resolution and the Tribunal's (NCLT's) confirmation.

stem: Under the pooling of interests method, the purchase consideration discharged by the transferee is ₹5,40,000 while the transferor's share capital is ₹5,00,000. The difference of ₹40,000 is:
options: Adjusted against (debited to) the reserves of the transferee
explanation: AS 14 requires the difference between consideration and the transferor's share capital to be adjusted in reserves; an excess is debited to reserves, with no goodwill created.

stem: Assertion (A): On forfeiture of shares, the share capital account is debited with the called-up amount and not merely the amount received.
reason: Reason (R): Forfeiture cancels the shares, so the entire called-up capital on them has to be removed from share capital.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Whole called-up capital on forfeited shares is cancelled; the amount paid goes to forfeiture account and the unpaid part to calls in arrears. R explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): When the cost of investment in a subsidiary is less than the parent's share in its net assets at acquisition, the difference is capital reserve on consolidation.
reason: Reason (R): A dividend received by the parent out of the subsidiary's pre-acquisition profits is treated as a capital receipt.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Both statements are true, but the treatment of pre-acquisition dividends is a separate rule and does not explain why a capital reserve arises.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Companies Act, 2013, a company cannot issue irredeemable preference shares.
reason: Reason (R): Redemption of preference shares is allowed only out of the proceeds of a fresh issue of shares and never out of profits.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is true as preference shares must be redeemable within a maximum of 20 years. R is false because redemption out of distributable profits is permitted.

stem: Assertion (A): A forfeited share may be reissued at a discount larger than the amount forfeited on it.
reason: Reason (R): The discount on reissue of forfeited shares cannot exceed the amount forfeited on those shares.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is false: R states the correct limit, so any discount must stay within the forfeited amount.

stem: Assertion (A): Where shares are bought back out of free reserves, an amount equal to the nominal value of the shares bought back is transferred to capital redemption reserve.
reason: Reason (R): This transfer ensures that the company's capital is not depleted by the buy-back, protecting creditors.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: CRR keeps the paid-up capital intact in effect, and R gives the purpose of the transfer, so it explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): In internal reconstruction, the company continues to exist after the scheme is implemented.
reason: Reason (R): In external reconstruction, the old company is wound up and a new company takes over its business.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Both statements are true, but the second describes a different type of reconstruction and does not explain the first.

stem: Consider the following statements regarding issue of shares under the Companies Act, 2013:
items: A company cannot issue shares at a discount, except sweat equity shares.
A company may issue shares at a premium.
Forfeited shares can never be reissued.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Section 53 prohibits issue at a discount (except sweat equity); premium is permitted; forfeited shares can be reissued.

stem: Consider the following statements about buy-back of shares:
items: The aggregate buy-back in a year is capped at 25 per cent of paid-up capital and free reserves.
The debt-equity ratio after buy-back must not be more than 2:1.
A buy-back may be made out of free reserves or securities premium.
Bought-back shares may be held as treasury shares and reissued at will.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Bought-back shares must be extinguished; a company cannot hold them as treasury shares.

stem: Consider the following statements about consolidation of accounts of a holding company:
items: Cost of control is the cost of investment less the parent's share of equity at acquisition.
Pre-acquisition profits of the subsidiary form part of consolidated revenue reserves.
Unrealised profit on intra-group stock is eliminated from consolidated stock.
Inter-company balances are shown as assets and liabilities in the consolidated balance sheet.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Pre-acquisition profits are capital profits and enter cost of control; inter-company balances are eliminated.

stem: Consider the following statements about types of corporate combination:
items: In absorption, an existing company takes over the business of another existing company.
In amalgamation proper, two or more companies are wound up and a new company is formed.
In absorption, a new company is always formed.
In external reconstruction, the old company is wound up and a new company takes over its business.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Absorption involves an existing acquirer, so no new company is needed; the other statements are correct.

stem: Consider the following statements about distribution of surplus in the winding up of a company:
items: Preferential creditors are paid before unsecured creditors.
The liquidator prepares a statement of receipts and payments.
After outside liabilities, preference shareholders are paid before equity shareholders.
Equity shareholders rank ahead of preference shareholders in repayment of capital.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Preference shareholders have a priority in return of capital over equity shareholders, so statement 4 is false.

stem: Consider the following statements about bonus shares:
items: They may be issued out of free reserves, securities premium or capital redemption reserve.
They bring fresh cash into the company.
Bonus shares cannot be issued in lieu of dividend.
The net worth of the company is unchanged by a bonus issue.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: A bonus issue capitalises reserves; it brings no cash and net worth is unchanged.

stem: Match List I (item) with List II (description):
listII: Created when preference shares or buy-back are funded out of profits
Excess of issue price over face value of shares
Amount received from shareholders before it is called
Called-up amount not yet paid by shareholders
explanation: Each item has its standard meaning in company accounts.

stem: Match List I (accounting standard of ICAI) with List II (subject):
listII: Accounting for amalgamations
Earnings per share
Accounting for investments
Consolidated financial statements
explanation: These are the subjects of the named Accounting Standards.

stem: Match List I (term in consolidation) with List II (meaning):
listII: Post-acquisition profit shared between holding company and minority
Outside shareholders' share in the subsidiary's net assets
Cost of investment less parent's share of equity at acquisition
Profit of the subsidiary earned before the date of acquisition
explanation: The terms describe goodwill/capital reserve, outsiders' share, pre-acquisition and post-acquisition profits.

stem: Match List I (term) with List II (feature):
listII: Ordered by the Tribunal
No declaration of solvency; creditors play the main role
Explains the reasons for shortfall shown by the statement of affairs
Directors make a declaration of solvency
explanation: Each term is matched with its standard feature.

stem: Arrange the following steps in the forfeiture of shares in the correct order:
items: Shareholder defaults in paying a call
Board passes a resolution forfeiting the shares
Forfeited shares are reissued
Board sends a notice demanding payment
explanation: Default, notice, forfeiture resolution, and finally reissue.

stem: Arrange the following stages of a public issue of shares in the correct order:
items: First call made
Allotment of shares
Application money received
Final call made
explanation: Application comes first, followed by allotment, the first call and the final call.

stem: Arrange the following steps in the books of the transferee in an amalgamation:
items: Record the takeover of assets and liabilities
Discharge the purchase consideration
Record goodwill or capital reserve
Determine the purchase consideration
explanation: Consideration is computed first, assets taken over, consideration discharged, and any difference recognised.

stem: Arrange the following steps in preparing a consolidated balance sheet in the correct order:
items: Combine balances after eliminating inter-company items
Compute cost of control
Separate pre-acquisition and post-acquisition profits of the subsidiary
Ascertain the holding company's and minority's share of the subsidiary
explanation: Shareholding is ascertained, profits are split, cost of control is computed, and finally balances are combined.

stem: A firm has current assets of ₹5,00,000, including inventory of ₹1,50,000 and prepaid expenses of ₹20,000. Its current liabilities are ₹2,00,000. Its quick (liquid) ratio is:
explanation: Quick assets = current assets − inventory − prepaid expenses = 5,00,000 − 1,50,000 − 20,000 = ₹3,30,000. Quick ratio = 3,30,000 ÷ 2,00,000 = 1.65. Excluding only inventory would give 1.75, ignoring the prepaid expenses.

stem: Credit sales for the year are ₹12,00,000. Trade receivables were ₹1,00,000 at the beginning and ₹1,40,000 at the end of the year. The debtors (receivables) turnover ratio is:
explanation: Average receivables = (1,00,000 + 1,40,000) ÷ 2 = ₹1,20,000. Turnover = 12,00,000 ÷ 1,20,000 = 10 times. Using only closing receivables gives 8.57 and using only opening gives 12.

stem: Which of the following is a source of funds in a funds flow statement prepared on the working-capital concept?
options: Sale of a long-term investment for cash
explanation: Sale of a non-current investment brings in working capital, so it is a source. Redemption of shares, dividend payment and purchase of machinery all consume working capital and are applications of funds.

stem: Which of the following transactions leaves the net working capital of a firm unchanged?
options: Sale of old machinery for cash
Issue of equity shares for cash
Payment of an interim dividend in cash
Payment to trade creditors in cash
explanation: Paying creditors reduces cash (a current asset) and creditors (a current liability) by the same amount, so working capital is unchanged. The other three each change one current item against a non-current item or an appropriation.

stem: A company has a net profit margin of 5%, a total asset turnover of 2 times and an equity multiplier (total assets ÷ equity) of 1.5. Using the DuPont identity, its return on equity is:
explanation: ROE = net profit margin × asset turnover × equity multiplier = 5% × 2 × 1.5 = 15%. The ROA is 10% (5% × 2); leverage raises it to 15%.

stem: A firm has total assets of ₹15,00,000 and total outside liabilities of ₹6,00,000. Its proprietary ratio is:
explanation: Shareholders' funds = 15,00,000 − 6,00,000 = ₹9,00,000. Proprietary ratio = shareholders' funds ÷ total assets = 9,00,000 ÷ 15,00,000 = 0.60. 0.40 is liabilities to assets; 1.5 is equity to outside liabilities.

stem: Profit before tax is ₹2,00,000 after depreciation of ₹30,000 and a profit on sale of machinery of ₹10,000. During the year trade receivables rose by ₹25,000, trade payables rose by ₹15,000 and inventory fell by ₹20,000. Cash generated from operations (before tax paid) is:
explanation: 2,00,000 + 30,000 (depreciation) − 10,000 (profit on sale, an investing item) = 2,20,000. Then −25,000 (receivables) + 15,000 (payables) + 20,000 (inventory) = ₹2,30,000.

stem: Profit before tax of ₹1,50,000 is stated after charging depreciation ₹30,000, preliminary expenses written off ₹5,000 and loss on sale of furniture ₹7,000, and after crediting profit on sale of investments ₹12,000. Funds from operations is:
explanation: Add back non-fund charges and non-operating losses: 1,50,000 + 30,000 + 5,000 + 7,000 = 1,92,000. Deduct non-operating profit of 12,000 to get ₹1,80,000.

stem: Net profit after tax is ₹5,00,000 and the preference dividend is ₹50,000. There are 1,00,000 equity shares and the market price per share is ₹90. The price-earnings ratio is:
explanation: EPS = (5,00,000 − 50,000) ÷ 1,00,000 = ₹4.50. P/E = 90 ÷ 4.50 = 20 times. Forgetting the preference dividend gives EPS ₹5 and P/E 18.

stem: Assertion (A): Common-size statements help to compare firms of different sizes.
reason: Reason (R): Each item in a common-size statement is expressed as a percentage of a common base such as net sales or total assets.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Converting figures to percentages of a common base removes the effect of absolute size, which is exactly why size-different firms become comparable.

stem: Assertion (A): A very high current ratio is not necessarily a sign of sound financial management.
reason: Reason (R): The current ratio is computed by dividing current assets by current liabilities.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is true because a high ratio may reflect idle cash, excess inventory or slow-moving receivables. R is a true definition but does not explain why a high value can be undesirable.

stem: Assertion (A): A funds flow statement based on the working-capital concept conveys the same information as a cash flow statement.
reason: Reason (R): The funds flow statement analyses changes in net working capital, whereas the cash flow statement analyses changes in cash and cash equivalents.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is false because the two statements have different bases: one explains movements in working capital, the other movements in cash. R correctly states that difference.

stem: Assertion (A): A lower debt-equity ratio is generally regarded as lower financial risk for creditors.
reason: Reason (R): A firm with a low debt-equity ratio can never face a liquidity problem.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is true: less debt means a smaller fixed-charge burden and more owners' cushion. R is false because liquidity depends on the current assets and current liabilities position, and a low-debt firm can still be short of cash.

stem: Assertion (A): Issue of bonus shares is not a source of funds in a funds flow statement.
reason: Reason (R): Bonus shares are issued by capitalising reserves, so no resources are received by the company.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The statement given as A is true (the Assertion is phrased in the negative), and R explains it: bonus issue only converts reserves into share capital without bringing in any working capital.

stem: Assertion (A): A firm adopting just-in-time purchasing is likely to show a higher inventory turnover ratio.
reason: Reason (R): Just-in-time purchasing reduces the average inventory held for a given cost of goods sold.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Inventory turnover = cost of goods sold ÷ average inventory. Lower average stock under JIT raises the ratio, so R directly explains A.

stem: Consider the following statements about comparative analysis of financial statements:
items: A common-size income statement expresses each item as a percentage of net sales.
In trend analysis, the figures of a base year are taken as 100.
Comparative statements show only the current year's figures.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Comparative statements place figures of two or more periods side by side, so statement 3 is false.

stem: Consider the following statements about the cash flow statement under Ind AS 7:
items: Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments readily convertible into known amounts of cash with insignificant risk of change in value.
Cash flows from operating activities may be reported by either the direct or the indirect method.
Acquisition of an asset by issuing shares is shown as a financing cash inflow.
Bank overdrafts repayable on demand that form an integral part of cash management may be included in cash and cash equivalents.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. A non-cash transaction such as an asset acquired against shares involves no cash flow and is excluded from the statement (disclosed elsewhere), so statement 3 is wrong.

stem: Consider the following statements about a funds flow statement:
items: A schedule of changes in working capital shows the changes in current assets and current liabilities.
Payment of dividend is shown as a source of funds.
Purchase of fixed assets for cash is an application of funds.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Dividend payment uses up funds and is an application, not a source.

stem: Consider the following statements about ratio classification:
items: Liquidity ratios measure the ability of a firm to meet its short-term obligations.
Activity ratios indicate how efficiently the firm uses its assets.
Interest coverage ratio is a profitability ratio.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Interest coverage is a coverage/solvency ratio, which tells whether earnings are sufficient to service interest; it is not a profitability ratio. Statements 1 and 2 are correct.

stem: Consider the following limitations of ratio analysis:
items: Ratios based on historical cost figures may not reflect current values.
Ratios of different firms are always comparable regardless of differing accounting policies.
Window dressing of the balance sheet can distort ratios.
Ratios are forecasts of future performance.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Ratios use past accounting data (so historical-cost and window-dressing problems arise). Different accounting policies reduce comparability, and ratios are not forecasts, so statements 2 and 4 are false.

stem: Consider the following statements about shareholder-oriented ratios:
items: Earnings per share = (net profit after tax − preference dividend) ÷ number of equity shares.
Dividend payout ratio = dividend per share ÷ earnings per share.
Return on equity is computed on total capital employed, including long-term loans.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: ROE uses equity shareholders' funds as the base, not total capital employed (that is ROCE). Statements 1 and 2 are correct.

stem: Match List I (ratio) with List II (formula):
listII: Dividend per share ÷ Earnings per share
Shareholders' funds ÷ Total assets
Net sales ÷ Net fixed assets
(Cash + marketable securities) ÷ Current liabilities
explanation: Absolute liquid ratio uses only cash and marketable securities; fixed assets turnover is sales over net fixed assets; proprietary ratio is owners' funds over total assets; payout ratio is DPS over EPS.

stem: Match List I (tool of financial analysis) with List II (description):
listII: Figures of two or more periods placed side by side with changes
Items expressed as an index relative to a base year taken as 100
Numerical relationships between related financial items
Each item shown as a percentage of a base total in the same statement
explanation: Each tool is matched to its defining feature.

stem: Match List I (DuPont component) with List II (what it reflects):
listII: Operating efficiency and profitability of sales
Overall return earned for the owners
Extent of financial leverage
Efficiency in using assets to generate sales
explanation: ROE = margin × asset turnover × equity multiplier; each factor reflects a different driver of owners' return.

stem: Match List I (term) with List II (meaning under Ind AS 7 / cash flow analysis):
listII: Excluded from the statement and disclosed separately
Reports major classes of gross cash receipts and gross cash payments
Adjusts profit for non-cash items and working-capital changes
Short-term, highly liquid investments with insignificant risk of value change
explanation: Direct method shows gross receipts and payments; indirect method reconciles profit to operating cash flow; cash equivalents are short-term liquid investments; non-cash transactions are disclosed elsewhere.

stem: Arrange the following steps of a ratio analysis exercise in the logical order:
items: Calculate the ratios from the financial statements
Determine the purpose of the analysis
Select the relevant ratios
Interpret the results and report conclusions
Compare the ratios with standards or past trends
explanation: Analysis begins with the objective, then selection, computation, comparison and finally interpretation.

stem: Arrange the following current assets in descending order of liquidity (most liquid first):
items: Trade receivables
Inventory
Marketable securities (short-term)
Cash in hand
explanation: Cash is most liquid, then readily saleable securities, then receivables (collected after credit period), and inventory the least liquid because it must first be sold.

stem: A firm has current assets of ₹3,00,000 (inventory ₹1,00,000, cash ₹30,000, marketable securities ₹20,000, receivables ₹1,50,000) and current liabilities of ₹1,50,000. Arrange the ratios in ascending order of value:
items: Absolute liquid ratio
Current ratio
Quick ratio

stem: Arrange the following steps in deriving net cash from operating activities by the indirect method:
items: Start with profit before tax
Adjust for changes in working capital
Add back non-cash items and deduct non-operating gains
Deduct income tax paid
